### Second Page

Paragraph one of the long run. Placeholder words follow one another in an orderly line, saying nothing at all, so that the page has enough text to run out of room. The sentences are invented for the test and carry no meaning beyond their length, which is the only thing the layout cares about.

Paragraph two of the long run. A test pattern needs bulk more than sense, so each sentence here is a little longer than it has to be, and each clause adds a few more words to push the column down toward the footer, where the furniture sits and the text must stop.

Paragraph three of the long run. When column one is full, the rest of the text moves to column two, below nothing at all, because this page carries its art in a band across both columns. When column two is full as well, the text moves to a page that the source never asked for.

Paragraph four of the long run. That extra page has no header and no art; it is two plain columns of whatever text was left over, with the footer drawn at the bottom as on every other page. The builder warns when this happens, but it still sets every word.

Paragraph five of the long run. More filler follows, in the same flat tone, with the same lack of content. Words such as lantern, ledger, harbour, orchard, chisel and meadow appear only to vary the line breaks, so that the paragraphs do not all end at the same place.

Paragraph six of the long run. The quick brown fox has retired from test patterns and left this paragraph to a slow grey heron, which stands in a shallow pond, looks at nothing in particular and waits for the paragraph to end so that the next one can begin.

Paragraph seven of the long run. Somewhere around here the second column of the second page fills up, though the exact line depends on the fonts and the band's height, which is why the tests measure the output rather than assume where any given sentence will land.

Another paragraph of the long run. It exists to make the run longer, which it does by being here at all, and by going on for a while about how it goes on for a while, which is the one subject a filler paragraph can always speak to with authority.

Yet another paragraph of the long run. By now the reader has stopped reading, which is fine, because the reader is a test, and the test reads only the positions of a few marked lines: where the card starts, where it ends, and which page each one sits on.

One more paragraph of the long run. It mentions a kettle, a lighthouse, a compass, a thimble and a weathervane, for no reason beyond giving the line breaker some longer words to wrap, and then it stops, as all good filler eventually must.

Paragraph eight of the long run. A card follows this paragraph. It must never split across columns or pages, so if it does not fit in the space left in a column it moves whole to the top of the next one, leaving a gap rather than cutting its frame in two.

Paragraph nine of the long run, after the card. It closes the fixture with a few more invented sentences, so that some text follows the card and the tests can see the flow carry on past an unbreakable box.
